new.definition: Oysters on the half shell covered with a rich green sauce and baked until hot, a dish created at Antoine’s in the French Quarter. The original recipe is a family secret, and Antoine’s chefs have said it holds no spinach. Most versions made since use spinach for the green. The Brennan’s Thanksgiving Day gratin of 2026 took the idea into creamed spinach, bacon and breadcrumbs.
new.guest: Oysters Rockefeller was born in the French Quarter at Antoine’s, in 1899 by most accounts, and named for John D. Rockefeller, the richest American of his day, for the richness of its green sauce. The recipe has long been kept a family secret. Our Thanksgiving Day gratin took the idea into oysters baked with bacon and creamed spinach under a crisp breadcrumb top.
new.kitchen: The classic is baked or broiled on the half shell until the topping browns and the dish comes out hot. Whether the Thanksgiving gratin was built in the shell or in one dish, and how many oysters went into a portion, was the kitchen’s to say.
new.compare: A raw oyster on the half shell comes to the table cold and as it is; oysters Rockefeller is baked under a green topping and served hot, so the oyster is cooked.

sources.title: Food Republic: How Oysters Rockefeller Were Created In 1899
Tasting Table: Oysters Rockefeller Was Named For The Richest Man In The World

new.background: Antoine’s opened in New Orleans in 1840 and is counted among the oldest family run restaurants in the United States. In 1899, by most accounts, the founder’s son, who had trained in France, found the snails he imported from France hard to come by and put local Gulf oysters under a rich green sauce in their place. He named the dish for John D. Rockefeller (1839 to 1937), the wealthiest American of the day, for the richness of the sauce; some accounts add that its green recalled paper money. The recipe stayed a family secret, and Antoine’s chefs have long said it holds no spinach, though most cooks since have used it. A few sources give the year as 1889.

new.definition: A dish baked or broiled until a browned crust forms on top, usually of breadcrumbs, cheese, butter or a mix of them. The word names the crust as much as the dish. It is usually made in a shallow dish, so more of what is underneath lies close to the crust. Potatoes, vegetables, pasta and seafood are all cooked this way.
new.guest: A gratin is anything baked until it wears a golden crust on top; the word comes from the French for to scrape, after the browned bits cooks scraped from the pan. On our Thanksgiving Day menu it was oysters with bacon and creamed spinach under breadcrumbs, baked until the top turned crisp.
new.kitchen: Topped with crumbs, cheese or butter and finished in a hot oven or under the broiler until the surface browns and the filling is hot through.
new.compare: Gratin dauphinois, the potato gratin of the Dauphiné, is by tradition made without cheese; au gratin in American usage often means with cheese, but the crust, not the cheese, is what the word names.

sources.title: Connexion France: The origins and meaning of gratin
Mon séjour en montagne: Le gratin dauphinois, le plat emblématique du Dauphiné

new.background: Gratin comes from the French verb gratter, to scrape, which goes back to a Germanic word for scratching. It first meant the browned crust that stuck to the bottom and sides of the pot, the part cooks scraped away, and only later the dish baked to make that crust on purpose. Merriam Webster dates the English phrase au gratin, literally with the scrapings, to 1806. The potato gratin of the Dauphiné, in southeastern France, is first recorded on 12 July 1788, when a gratin was served at a dinner the province’s lieutenant general gave for the municipal officials of Gap, though the dish is surely older; by tradition it holds no cheese. In French, le gratin has also come to mean the upper crust of society, the choice top of the dish.

new.definition: Cured pork belly, usually smoked, sold as a slab or sliced into strips. In the United States the word alone means the belly; bacon from another cut or animal must say so, as pork shoulder bacon or turkey bacon do. The cure is salt, usually with nitrite and often sugar and spice, rubbed on dry or pumped in, and the belly is then smoked or heat processed. Bacon sold with no other description is raw and must be cooked.
new.guest: Bacon is pork belly cured with salt and usually smoked, which gives it its smoky, salty flavor. On our Thanksgiving Day menu it went into the Rockefeller Gratin and was wrapped around the pork tenderloin, where its fat protects the lean meat in the oven.
new.kitchen: Rendered until its fat runs and the meat crisps, or wrapped around a lean cut so its fat protects the meat in the oven. Which bacon the kitchen buys, and how it was smoked, is a question for the chef.
new.compare: Pancetta is cured belly too, but usually unsmoked; salt pork is fattier and is not smoked, so it is not bacon.

sources.title: USDA FSIS: Bacon and Food Safety
Tasting Table: Salt Pork Vs Bacon

new.background: The word reached English in the Middle Ages through Old French, which took it from a Germanic word for the back, and at first it meant a side of pork or a ham rather than the strips of today. In colonial America the farms that kept pigs kept smokehouses too. Hogs were butchered in early winter, when the meat would not spoil before it was cured, then salted and hung over a slow fire so the bellies became bacon and the legs ham. Traditional smoking of bacon took many days. Mass production moved much of it to convection ovens, which the USDA notes can finish a batch in as little as six hours. Federal labeling keeps the plain name for cured belly.

new.definition: Wild shrimp caught in the Gulf, almost all of them one of three species: brown, white and pink. Brown and white shrimp come mainly from Louisiana and Texas waters; pink shrimp mostly from the west coast of Florida. In Louisiana’s inside waters brown shrimp are the catch of the spring season and white shrimp of the fall season. Species, size and where they were landed are on the supplier’s record.
new.guest: Gulf shrimp are wild shrimp from the bays and coastal waters of Louisiana and its neighbors, with a sweet, briny bite. They go into our seafood gumbo, and on the Thanksgiving Day menu they also went into the shrimp sauce piquante and the BBQ shrimp stuffing. Where tonight’s shrimp were landed is the kitchen’s to say.
new.kitchen: Peeled, often deveined, and added near the end of a dish so they stay tender; the shells can go into the stock.
new.compare: Brown and white shrimp are different species with different Louisiana seasons, brown in spring and early summer and white in the fall; the label, not the shell color, says which it is.

sources.title: Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries: Shrimp Season
WWNO: How a New Orleans immigrant created a global dried shrimp business
National Park Service, Jean Lafitte: Ranger Recipes, Seafood

new.background: NOAA counts white shrimp as the first commercially important shrimp in the United States, fished as far back as 1709, and reports that almost all the white and brown shrimp the country harvests come from the Gulf, mainly off Louisiana and Texas. Part of the Louisiana catch was once dried in the sun. Chinese fishermen are credited with bringing commercial shrimp drying to Louisiana in the 1870s, spreading boiled shrimp across broad wooden platforms built on stilts above the marsh. Manila Village, which Filipino settlers built in Barataria Bay in the late 1800s, was the largest of those platform villages until Hurricane Betsy destroyed it in 1965. Louisiana has generally set its inshore seasons by species, brown shrimp from about May into July and white shrimp from about mid August into December.

new.definition: A swimming crab of the Atlantic coast of the Americas and the Gulf, and the crab of Louisiana’s crabmeat. Picked meat is sold by grade: jumbo lump, the large white pieces from the two muscles that drive the swimming legs; lump, smaller and broken white pieces; and claw meat, darker and stronger in flavor. Grade names and piece sizes vary from packer to packer, so the packer’s description matters. A blue crab taken just after it molts is sold whole as a soft-shell crab.
new.guest: Blue crab is the sweet, delicate crab of the Gulf and the Atlantic coast; its Latin name means beautiful savory swimmer. In our seafood gumbo it adds a gentle sweetness against the smoky andouille and the brine of the oysters.
new.kitchen: Bought as picked meat by grade or as live crabs; large white lumps are folded in gently near the end so they stay whole. Which grade goes into the gumbo is the kitchen’s to say.
new.compare: Jumbo lump is the large white meat of the swimming leg muscles, kept whole for presentation; claw meat is darker and stronger, and suits soups and bisques.

new.background: The blue crab was described and named in 1896 as Callinectes sapidus, from Greek words for beautiful and swimmer and the Latin for savory, so its name reads beautiful savory swimmer. It is native to the Atlantic coast of the Americas from Nova Scotia to northern Argentina, the Gulf included, and Louisiana’s crabbers have long worked its estuaries: the state’s 2014 management plan called Louisiana’s the largest blue crab fishery in the country, landing more than half the blue crab taken in the Gulf. Crabs grow by molting. Louisiana shedders hold peeler crabs in tanks until they slip their old shells and sell them as soft-shell crabs, a trade that has since shrunk.

deepen.background: The oyster of the Gulf is the eastern oyster, Crassostrea virginica, the same species that grows along the Atlantic coast, and it thrives in estuaries where river water meets the sea. In Louisiana the trade owes much to Croatian immigrants. Through the nineteenth century men from villages on the Dalmatian coast of the Adriatic, such as Duba, settled in Plaquemines Parish fishing towns like Olga, Empire and Buras, and they are widely credited with building the state’s commercial oyster industry. New Orleans cooks took the oyster in every direction: raw on the half shell, fried, simmered in gumbo and baked, as in oysters Rockefeller, created at Antoine’s in the French Quarter in 1899 by most accounts.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Rockefeller Gratin and Seafood Gumbo
deepen.guest: Gulf oysters are the eastern oyster, the same species that grows along the Atlantic coast, and they can taste sweet, briny or a little of both, depending on where they grew. They go into our seafood gumbo, and on the Thanksgiving Day menu they were baked into the Rockefeller Gratin.

deepen.background: Smoking is one of the old ways of keeping meat, though salt did much of the keeping while smoke added aroma and color. In colonial Virginia the smokehouse was a fixture of farm and plantation: the earliest known use of the word, written smoak house, is a 1716 record from York County, and hogs killed in early winter were salted, then hung over a slow fire for one to two weeks. Hickory, apple and maple are the woods the USDA names for the most satisfactory smoke flavor. In Louisiana, andouille makers of the River Parishes smoke their sausage hard, often over pecan wood. Hot smoking cooks as it flavors; cold smoking does not.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: the andouille in the Seafood Gumbo, and the bacon in the Rockefeller Gratin and around the Bacon-Wrapped Pork Tenderloin
deepen.guest: Smoked means flavored by the fumes of smoldering hardwood, which gives meat a deep, savory aroma and a darker color. The smoke comes through the andouille in our seafood gumbo, and on the Thanksgiving Day menu it came through the bacon in the gratin and around the pork tenderloin; which wood each producer uses is a question for the kitchen.
